title: Change Point Localization in Dynamic Multilayer Networks
one_liner: A method to find exactly when a network's connection patterns shift by splitting the timeline and checking layer-specific changes.
lead: Networks change over time—friendships form and fade, trade routes open and close, neural circuits rewire. This paper solves the problem of finding the exact moments when a multilayer network (where different types of connections exist between the same set of people or things) switches to a new pattern. Unlike past work, it gives both precise locations and reliable confidence intervals.

problem.h2: Finding the moment a network's structure breaks
paras: Consider a social network where people connect through different channels: direct chat, group projects, shared interests. The pattern of who talks to whom can shift suddenly—maybe a team reorganizes, a community fractures, or a natural disaster forces new routes. You have a long history of snapshots of the network at each time step, but you want to know: when exactly did the structure change? A naive approach would check every time point individually, looking at sudden jumps in connection counts, but this is unreliable because random noise makes every snapshot look slightly different. You need a principled way to separate real structural breaks from daily fluctuations.

callout.html: Split the timeline recursively to locate change points, then use tensor estimation (fitting a multi-dimensional array capturing all layers and time steps) to refine each location by borrowing information across all layers at once.

panels.title: 2. Naive splitting
panels.caption: Split the timeline into chunks, test each one for a change. Many false alarms.

panels.title: 3. Binary segmentation finds rough breaks
panels.caption: Recursively split where the signal changes most. Narrow down to near the break.

panels.title: 4. Tensor refinement across layers
panels.caption: Sharpen the location by fitting all layers simultaneously. One true moment emerges.

panels.title: 5. Confidence interval
panels.caption: The refined estimate sits at the peak, with width showing uncertainty.

steps.text: Collect snapshots of the multilayer network at T time steps.
At each interval, find the time point that splits the data to maximize a dissimilarity score. Keep splitting until no more breaks are found.
You now have a list of rough locations where the structure likely changed.
For each rough location, fit a low-rank model using all layers at once to pinpoint the exact moment.
Use the fitted model to estimate how uncertain each refined location is.

paras: The paper focuses on finding the exact time points (change points) where the connection patterns of a dynamic multilayer network shift. It refines coarse estimates by using information from all layers at the same time, rather than analyzing each layer separately.

hidden.name: Low-rank shared basis of the network
paras: In a multilayer random dot product graph, each connection between two people is determined by their shared hidden positions (latent coordinates) and layer-specific patterns applied to those positions. The paper identifies and estimates this shared low-rank structure to refine where the break occurs. Specifically, near a true change point, the network's layer-specific patterns suddenly shift, but the underlying node positions evolve smoothly. By fitting the best low-rank model in a narrow window, the method finds the exact time when the layer-specific patterns 'jump', because that is when the residual error drops most sharply.

heat.caption: Darker means higher explained variance. Highlights show quantities that shift at the change point.

reads.html: The network's connections come from hidden positions shared by all layers, combined with layer-specific multipliers. When a break happens, those multipliers change suddenly. The method finds the exact moment by looking for where a low-rank fit gets much better.

The D-MRDPG model assumes each connection probability depends on shared latent node positions and time-varying, layer-specific factor loading matrices. A change point occurs when these loadings shift. Low-rank tensor estimation recovers the factor structure, and refinement identifies the time point minimizing the reconstruction error.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Recursive refinement with shared structure
paras: The method works in two stages. First, binary segmentation is a greedy algorithm that splits the timeline and tests whether each half has a different pattern. It keeps recursively splitting (always at the point that minimizes the within-segment error) until no more statistically significant breaks appear. This gives rough locations fast but is not always precise, because noise can cause small shifts even without a real change.

Second, the method refines each rough candidate by fitting a low-rank tensor model (a multi-dimensional array capturing connections across time and layers) in a tight window around it. At a true change point, the layer-specific patterns (the factors in the low-rank model) shift abruptly, but the shared node positions do not. So fitting a single model on each side of the candidate time, then comparing, reveals where the fit error drops most dramatically. That is the true change point. The two-stage approach is much faster and more accurate than brute-force search, because binary segmentation narrows the search space, and tensor fitting pinpoints the exact location by using all layers at once instead of one at a time.

stages.s: Multilayer network snapshots from time 1 to T
Recursive binary segmentation finds rough break candidates
For each candidate, fit low-rank tensor to left segment
Fit low-rank tensor to right segment
Find time point where refitted model error drops most
Refined change point locations with confidence intervals

math.words: For a candidate change point, fit the layer-specific factors and shared node positions to minimize the squared difference between the observed network and the predicted network from the low-rank model.
math.equation: min_{U,V_1,...,V_L} sum_{l,i,j} (A_{l,ij,t} - U_i * V_l * U_j)^2 for t in [tau, tau+delta]
symbols: connection between node i and node j on layer l at time t (1 = connected, 0 = not)
shared latent position of node i (a list of numbers)
layer-specific multiplier for layer l (a number or small matrix)
window size around the candidate (e.g., 10 or 50 time steps)
find the values of U and V that make the error as small as possible

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say we have 3 nodes and 2 layers. Node pair (i,j) has shared latent positions U_i=[0.5, 0.3] and U_j=[0.4, 0.2].
Layer 1 multiplier V_1 = 2.0. Predicted connection Layer 1: (0.5*0.4 + 0.3*0.2) * 2.0 = (0.20 + 0.06) * 2.0 = 0.52.
Observed connection Layer 1: 1.0. Error for this pair on this layer: (1.0 - 0.52)^2 = 0.2304.
Repeat for all pairs and layers, sum the squared errors. Change point is where the sum is lowest on one side, highest on the other.

math.note: The method finds the time point where the low-rank factors fit most abruptly change, revealing the hidden structural break.

charts.title: Naive method (point-by-point test)
charts.note: Tests each time independently, missing the shared structure across layers.

charts.title: This paper (two-stage refinement)
charts.note: Binary segmentation + tensor refinement pinpoints changes with few false positives.

items.b: Too many time steps, very sparse data.
items.html: If the network is mostly empty (few connections), the low-rank fit becomes unreliable. Noise dominates, and the method may hallucinate change points. Requires a minimum density of connections.

items.b: Gradual drift instead of abrupt jumps.
items.html: If the connection patterns shift slowly (not suddenly), the method is designed for abrupt structural breaks and will mislocalize or miss the transition entirely. The math assumes a jump in the layer-specific patterns.

If you choose too high a rank (too many latent dimensions), the model overfits and flags noise as breaks. Too low a rank and you miss the real structure. The method requires tuning this hyperparameter carefully.
The method works best on moderately dense multilayer networks with genuine abrupt structural shifts, given proper tuning of the low-rank dimension and refinement window size.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple synthetic dynamic network: create 20 nodes with a fixed latent position model for times 1–30. At time 31, suddenly change all the layer-specific multipliers (e.g., swap which connections are likely). Continue to time 60 with the new multipliers. Run the two-stage algorithm and plot the refinement locations. The true change point is time 31. Measure how close the refined estimate is to the truth, and show that adding noise (random edges) makes the localization wider but still centered near 31. Show confidence intervals that contain the true break.
demo.metric_eq: Average error = abs(estimated_change_point - true_change_point); Confidence interval width = abs(upper_bound - lower_bound)
demo.closing: The demo must show that the refined estimate is within 2 time steps of the true break and that the confidence interval captures it.
